lessons.title: Tell me about yourself
lessons.interviewAnswer: Use a 60–90 second present → past → future structure. Start with your current professional identity, connect 2–3 relevant experiences, and end with the type of problem you want to solve next. Do not narrate the entire CV.
keyPoints: Choose experiences that support the target role

lessons.title: Defend Any Technical Project
lessons.interviewAnswer: Explain projects as problem → constraints → approach → your contribution → evaluation → result → limitations → what you would improve. Interviewers often care more about why you made a choice than the final architecture.
keyPoints: Know every metric on your CV
State limitations before the interviewer discovers them
Be ready to productionize the prototype

lessons.title: Behavioral Answers with CAR / STAR
lessons.interviewAnswer: Use Context, Action, Result (or STAR) to keep behavioral answers concrete. Spend most of the time on your own action and the measurable result, then add what changed in your behavior afterward.
keyPoints: End failure stories with changed behavior

lessons.title: How to Handle a Question You Do Not Know
lessons.interviewAnswer: Do not bluff. State what you know, identify the uncertain part, reason from first principles, and describe how you would verify it. A structured partial answer is usually stronger than confident guessing.
keyPoints: Ask one clarifying question only when necessary
Never invent metrics or implementation details

lessons.title: Lists, Tuples, Sets & Dictionaries
lessons.interviewAnswer: Choose the data structure based on semantics and complexity: lists preserve order and allow duplicates, tuples are immutable records, sets provide fast membership and uniqueness, and dictionaries map keys to values.

lessons.title: Iterators & Generators
lessons.interviewAnswer: Generators produce values lazily using yield, so they are useful when data is large or streaming and you do not want to hold the entire result in memory.

lessons.title: Decorators & Context Managers
lessons.interviewAnswer: Decorators wrap functions or classes to add behavior without changing the core implementation. Context managers guarantee setup/cleanup around a block, commonly for files, locks and resources.

lessons.title: NumPy Vectorization & Broadcasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vectorization moves loops into optimized native operations over arrays. Broadcasting lets arrays with compatible shapes interact without explicitly copying data.
keyPoints: Avoid Python loops for large numeric workloads

lessons.title: pandas: Merge, GroupBy, Missing Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: For data interviews, be able to load, filter, aggregate, join and reshape tables, then handle missing values deliberately rather than mechanically dropping or filling everything.

lessons.title: Testing ML / Data Code
lessons.interviewAnswer: Test deterministic transformation logic with unit tests, data assumptions with validation tests, and model behavior with slice or regression tests. Production ML needs tests around code, data and models.

lessons.title: SQL Joins
lessons.interviewAnswer: INNER JOIN returns matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left side and fills unmatched right-side columns with NULL; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows from both sides. Choose based on what records must survive the join.

visual.title: Join semantics
visual.caption: Always reason from table grain and which records must survive.

lessons.title: GROUP BY, HAVING & Aggregation
lessons.interviewAnswer: GROUP BY changes the grain of the result by aggregating rows into groups. WHERE filters before aggregation; HAVING filters after aggregation.

lessons.title: Window Functions
lessons.interviewAnswer: Window functions compute values across related rows without collapsing them. Common examples are ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD and running aggregates using OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...).

visual.title: Window Functions
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: CTEs & Subqueries
lessons.interviewAnswer: CTEs make complex SQL easier to reason about by naming intermediate results. They are often used to structure transformations before the final query.

lessons.title: Transactions & Indexes
lessons.interviewAnswer: Transactions group operations into an atomic unit with ACID guarantees. Indexes speed reads by maintaining an auxiliary search structure, but they consume storage and make writes more expensive.

visual.title: Indexed query path
visual.caption: An index can reduce the amount of data scanned, at the cost of storage and write overhead.

lessons.title: Stored Procedures & Data Pipelines
lessons.interviewAnswer: Stored procedures package database-side logic such as selection, joins and transformations. In data pipelines, orchestration tools can call these procedures and move their outputs to downstream stages.

lessons.title: Vectors, Matrices & Dot Products
lessons.interviewAnswer: A vector represents an ordered set of features or a direction; a matrix represents a linear transformation or collection of vectors. The dot product measures alignment and is the core operation behind linear models, attention scores and neural layers.

visual.title: Linear transformation
visual.caption: A matrix can be viewed as a transformation that rotates, scales, projects or mixes coordinates.

lessons.title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors & SVD
lessons.interviewAnswer: Eigenvectors are directions preserved by a linear transformation up to scaling. SVD decomposes any matrix into orthogonal directions and singular values, making it useful for compression, PCA intuition and low-rank approximation.

visual.title: SVD decomposition
visual.caption: SVD decomposes a linear map into orthogonal directions and axis-wise scaling.

lessons.title: Derivatives, Gradients & Chain Rule
lessons.interviewAnswer: A derivative measures local change; a gradient collects partial derivatives and points toward steepest increase. Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule through a computation graph.

visual.title: Gradient as local direction
visual.caption: The gradient points toward steepest local increase; optimization usually moves in the negative-gradient direction.

lessons.title: Convexity & Optimization Intuition
lessons.interviewAnswer: A convex objective has no bad local minima: any local minimum is global. Deep networks are non-convex, so optimization relies on practical gradient methods rather than global-optimum guarantees.

lessons.title: Gradient Descent & Learning Rate
lessons.interviewAnswer: Gradient descent updates parameters in the negative-gradient direction. Too large a learning rate can overshoot or diverge; too small a rate makes optimization painfully slow.

visual.title: Optimization trajectory
visual.caption: A good learning rate reduces loss steadily; too large can oscillate or diverge.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability & Bayes Rule
lessons.interviewAnswer: Conditional probability updates the probability of an event given evidence. Bayes rule reverses a conditional using prior probability and likelihood, and underlies probabilistic inference and many classifiers.

visual.title: Probability building blocks
visual.caption: Concept map for quick revision.

lessons.title: Common Probability Distributions
lessons.interviewAnswer: Know when Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Normal and related distributions are appropriate. The distribution is a model for the data-generating process, not merely a curve-fitting choice.

visual.title: Distribution shapes
visual.caption: Different distributions encode different assumptions about uncertainty and tail behavior.

lessons.title: Expectation, Variance & Covariance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Expectation is the long-run average of a random variable; variance measures spread around the mean; covariance measures how two variables vary together, with correlation providing a normalized version.

visual.title: Expectation, Variance & Covariance
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Law of Large Numbers & Central Limit Theorem
lessons.interviewAnswer: The law of large numbers explains why sample averages stabilize around expectations. The CLT explains why normalized sums often approach a Normal distribution, enabling many confidence intervals and tests.

visual.title: Central Limit Theorem intuition
visual.caption: Under broad conditions, the distribution of sample means becomes approximately normal as sample size grows.

lessons.title: Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A frequentist 95% confidence interval is produced by a procedure that would contain the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. It is not literally a 95% probability statement about a fixed parameter after observing the data.

visual.title: Confidence interval around an estimate
visual.caption: The interval is produced by a procedure with a stated long-run coverage rate; it is not a probability that this fixed interval contains the parameter.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing & p-values
lessons.interviewAnswer: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis and test assumptions are true, of seeing a result at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

visual.title: Null distribution and rejection region
visual.caption: A p-value measures how extreme the observed statistic is under the null model; the rejection region lives in the tails.

lessons.title: A/B Testing & Statistical Power
lessons.interviewAnswer: A/B testing compares randomized groups to estimate causal treatment effects. Before running the test, define the primary metric, minimum detectable effect, significance level and required power to determine sample size.

visual.title: A/B experiment
visual.caption: Randomization breaks systematic confounding in expectation, enabling a causal comparison.

lessons.title: MLE vs MAP
lessons.interviewAnswer: Maximum likelihood chooses parameters that make observed data most likely. MAP adds a prior and chooses the most probable parameters after combining prior and likelihood; many regularizers can be interpreted as MAP priors.

lessons.title: Linear Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of features and typically minimizes squared error. Know its assumptions, how coefficients are interpreted, and why multicollinearity/outliers can matter.

visual.title: Linear regression
visual.caption: The model estimates a conditional mean relationship; residual diagnostics matter as much as the fitted line.

lessons.title: Logistic Regression
lessons.interviewAnswer: Logistic regression models log-odds as a linear function of features and maps them through a sigmoid to a probability. Training usually minimizes log loss rather than MSE.

visual.title: Logistic decision function
visual.caption: Logistic regression maps a linear score through the sigmoid to obtain a probability between 0 and 1.

lessons.title: Decision Trees
lessons.interviewAnswer: Decision trees recursively split the feature space to make child nodes purer. They capture nonlinear interactions and require little preprocessing, but deep trees overfit easily.

visual.title: Decision tree
visual.caption: Trees recursively partition feature space into regions with simpler predictions.

lessons.title: Random Forest
lessons.interviewAnswer: Random forests reduce tree variance by training many trees on bootstrapped samples and random feature subsets, then averaging or voting their predictions.

visual.title: Random forest
visual.caption: Bagging and feature randomness reduce variance relative to a single deep tree.

lessons.title: Gradient Boosting / XGBoost Intuition
lessons.interviewAnswer: Boosting builds weak learners sequentially so each new learner focuses on correcting the current ensemble’s errors. Modern gradient-boosted trees are often excellent baselines for tabular data.

visual.title: Gradient boosting
items: Fit next learner to residual/gradient signal
visual.caption: Boosting builds a strong model sequentially by correcting errors made by the current ensemble.

lessons.title: Support Vector Machines
lessons.interviewAnswer: An SVM finds a decision boundary with maximum margin. Kernel functions allow nonlinear boundaries by computing similarity in an implicit higher-dimensional feature space.

visual.title: Maximum-margin classifier
visual.caption: An SVM chooses a separating boundary with maximum margin; kernels allow nonlinear boundaries.

lessons.title: k-Nearest Neighbors
lessons.interviewAnswer: k-NN predicts using nearby training examples. It is simple and non-parametric but sensitive to feature scaling, irrelevant dimensions and inference cost on large datasets.

lessons.title: Naive Bayes
lessons.interviewAnswer: Naive Bayes applies Bayes rule while assuming features are conditionally independent given the class. Despite the strong assumption, it can work surprisingly well for text and sparse features.

lessons.title: K-means Clustering
lessons.interviewAnswer: K-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and updating each centroid to the mean of its assigned points. It works best for roughly spherical clusters under the chosen distance metric.

visual.title: K-means clustering
visual.caption: K-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroid locations.

lessons.title: PCA
lessons.interviewAnswer: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance and projects data onto the leading components. It is useful for compression, visualization and removing correlated dimensions, but components are linear combinations of original features.

visual.title: PCA finds high-variance directions
visual.caption: The first principal component is the direction that captures the most variance in the data.

lessons.title: Bias–Variance Trade-off
lessons.interviewAnswer: High bias means the model is too constrained and underfits; high variance means it fits training data but changes too much with the sample and generalizes poorly. Model complexity, regularization and data size shift this balance.

visual.title: Bias–variance trade-off
visual.caption: As model complexity grows, training error usually falls while validation error can eventually rise.

lessons.title: MSE vs MAE
lessons.interviewAnswer: Use MSE when you want large errors penalized disproportionately because errors are squared. Use MAE when you want a loss that grows linearly and is more robust to outliers. The choice is about error behavior—not whether the current loss value is “large” or “small.”

visual.title: How error size changes the penalty
visual.caption: MAE grows linearly with residual magnitude; MSE grows quadratically, so large errors receive much more weight.

lessons.title: Precision, Recall & F1
lessons.interviewAnswer: Precision asks: of predicted positives, how many were correct? Recall asks: of actual positives, how many did we find? F1 is the harmonic mean and is useful when both matter, but the right metric depends on error costs.
keyPoints: False positive vs false negative cost

visual.title: Confusion matrix
visual.caption: Precision focuses on positive predictions; recall focuses on actual positives. The matrix makes the error types explicit.

lessons.title: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
lessons.interviewAnswer: ROC-AUC measures ranking across true-positive and false-positive rates. PR-AUC focuses on precision/recall and is often more informative when the positive class is rare and practically important.

visual.title: ROC and precision–recall views
visual.caption: ROC plots TPR vs FPR across thresholds. For rare positives, precision–recall curves often make the useful trade-off more visible.

lessons.title: Train/Validation/Test & Cross-validation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Use training data to fit parameters, validation data to make modeling choices, and test data only for final unbiased evaluation. Cross-validation estimates performance more robustly when data is limited.

visual.title: K-fold cross-validation
visual.caption: Each fold becomes validation once while the others train; time-series and grouped data require specialized splitting.

lessons.title: Data Leakage
lessons.interviewAnswer: Leakage occurs when training uses information that would not be available at prediction time or when related samples cross data splits. It produces deceptively good offline metrics and poor production performance.

visual.title: Leakage path
visual.caption: Leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time enters training or validation features.

lessons.title: Class Imbalance
lessons.interviewAnswer: For rare positives, accuracy can be meaningless. Use metrics aligned with the positive-class cost, consider class weights or resampling, preserve representative validation data, and tune the decision threshold.

visual.title: Accuracy can mislead on imbalanced data
visual.caption: A model that predicts only the majority class can look accurate while completely failing on the rare class.

lessons.title: Missing Values & Outliers
lessons.interviewAnswer: First ask why values are missing or extreme. Choose deletion, imputation, missingness indicators or robust transformations based on the data-generating process and model, not a blanket rule.

lessons.title: Feature Importance & Explainability
lessons.interviewAnswer: Feature importance can mean different things: model-specific impurity scores, permutation importance, SHAP-style local/global explanations, or coefficients. Interpret with care when features are correlated.

lessons.title: Neural Network Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A neural network composes linear transformations with nonlinear activations. Training adjusts parameters to minimize a loss, while intermediate layers learn representations useful for the task.

visual.title: Feed-forward neural network
visual.caption: Each layer applies a learned affine transformation followed by a nonlinearity, enabling hierarchical representation learning.

lessons.title: Backpropagation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Backpropagation efficiently computes gradients by applying the chain rule from the loss backward through the computation graph. The optimizer then uses those gradients to update parameters.

visual.title: Backpropagation
visual.caption: Backprop computes parameter gradients; the optimizer uses them to update weights.

lessons.title: Activation Functions
lessons.interviewAnswer: Nonlinear activations let deep networks represent nonlinear functions. ReLU-like functions are common in hidden layers; sigmoid/softmax are often used at outputs depending on the task.

visual.title: Activation functions
visual.caption: Nonlinear activations let stacked layers represent nonlinear functions.

lessons.title: SGD, Momentum & Adam
lessons.interviewAnswer: SGD follows noisy mini-batch gradients; momentum smooths updates by accumulating velocity; Adam adapts step sizes using first and second gradient moments. No optimizer is universally best.

visual.title: SGD vs Adam
visual.caption: Optimizer choice interacts with learning-rate schedules, batch size and model family.

lessons.title: Dropout, Weight Decay & Early Stopping
lessons.interviewAnswer: These techniques reduce overfitting in different ways: dropout injects stochastic feature removal, weight decay penalizes large parameters, and early stopping limits training when validation stops improving.

lessons.title: BatchNorm vs LayerNorm
lessons.interviewAnswer: BatchNorm normalizes using batch statistics and is common in CNNs; LayerNorm normalizes features within each example and is standard in transformers. Their behavior at inference differs.

visual.title: Normalization placement
visual.caption: Normalization stabilizes activation scales; BatchNorm and LayerNorm normalize along different axes.

lessons.title: Vanishing / Exploding Gradients
lessons.interviewAnswer: Repeated multiplication through deep networks can shrink or amplify gradients. Initialization, normalization, ReLU-like activations, residual connections and gradient clipping help depending on the architecture.

visual.title: Gradient through depth
visual.caption: Repeated multiplications can shrink gradients toward zero; residual connections and normalization help preserve signal.

lessons.title: Debugging a Model That Will Not Learn
lessons.interviewAnswer: Verify data and labels, then try to overfit a tiny batch. Inspect loss, outputs, gradients, learning rate, preprocessing and train/eval modes before changing architecture. Debug from simplest assumptions outward.

visual.title: Debugging a Model That Will Not Learn
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: CNN Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: CNNs exploit local spatial structure with shared filters. Early layers learn local edges/textures, while deeper layers combine them into larger receptive-field features.

visual.title: CNN hierarchy
visual.caption: Convolution combines local connectivity and weight sharing, building progressively richer spatial features.

lessons.title: Receptive Field
lessons.interviewAnswer: A unit’s receptive field is the input region that can influence it. Deeper layers, larger kernels, stride and dilation increase receptive field and therefore spatial context.

visual.title: Receptive field growth
visual.caption: Stacking convolutions increases the input region that can influence a feature.

lessons.title: Residual Networks
lessons.interviewAnswer: Residual connections learn a change relative to the input and create shorter gradient paths, making very deep networks easier to optimize.

visual.title: Residual block
visual.caption: Skip connections provide a direct information/gradient path through deep networks.

lessons.title: U-Net & Segmentation
lessons.interviewAnswer: U-Net combines an encoder that captures context with a decoder that restores spatial resolution, using skip connections to preserve fine localization information.

visual.title: U-Net encoder–decoder
visual.caption: U-Net combines a contracting encoder with a decoder and skip connections that restore fine spatial detail.

lessons.title: 2D vs 3D CNNs
lessons.interviewAnswer: 2D convolutions model height and width, while 3D convolutions also model depth and can learn cross-slice volumetric context directly. The trade-off is dramatically higher memory and compute.

visual.title: 2D vs 3D convolution
visual.caption: The right choice depends on whether the third dimension carries meaningful local structure and whether compute allows volumetric processing.

lessons.title: Vision Transformers
lessons.interviewAnswer: A ViT splits an image into patches, embeds them as tokens, adds positional information and applies transformer blocks. Attention gives global interactions, while CNNs have stronger built-in locality.

visual.title: Vision Transformer
visual.caption: ViT turns image patches into a token sequence and uses global self-attention instead of convolutional filters.

lessons.title: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS & FID
lessons.interviewAnswer: PSNR measures pixel-level fidelity, SSIM compares structural similarity, LPIPS uses deep features for perceptual similarity, and FID compares distributions of generated and real features. No single metric captures physical correctness.

visual.title: PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS & FID
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Super-resolution & Reconstruction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Super-resolution infers a higher-resolution signal from limited observations. The central tension is recovering detail without hallucinating unsupported structure, so downstream/domain validation is often essential.

lessons.title: Embeddings
lessons.interviewAnswer: Embeddings map discrete objects such as words, products or code into dense vectors where geometry captures learned relationships. They support similarity search, retrieval and neural-network inputs.

visual.title: Embedding space
visual.caption: Embeddings place items with similar learned meaning near each other according to a training objective.

lessons.title: Tokenization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Tokenization converts text into a sequence of discrete token IDs. Subword methods balance vocabulary size and sequence length and must match the model’s training tokenizer exactly.

visual.title: Tokenization
visual.caption: Tokenization converts text into discrete units that map to model vocabulary IDs.

lessons.title: Self-Attention: Q, K, V
lessons.interviewAnswer: Self-attention lets each token build a context-dependent representation by comparing its query with other tokens’ keys and taking a weighted combination of their values.

visual.title: Self-attention weight map
visual.caption: Each query token assigns a normalized weight distribution over key tokens; the weighted values form the output.

lessons.title: Transformer Architecture
lessons.interviewAnswer: Transformers combine attention, feed-forward networks, residual connections and normalization. Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants serve different tasks.

visual.title: Transformer block
visual.caption: Transformer layers alternate attention-based context mixing with position-wise feed-forward computation.

lessons.title: BERT vs GPT-style Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: BERT-style models are typically encoder-only and learn bidirectional contextual representations; GPT-style models are decoder-only and autoregressively predict the next token. Their pretraining objectives drive different strengths.

visual.title: BERT vs GPT training
visual.caption: The attention mask and training objective shape what the model learns to do.

lessons.title: Positional Information
lessons.interviewAnswer: Attention itself is permutation-invariant, so transformers need positional information. Systems may use learned embeddings, sinusoidal encodings or relative/rotary approaches such as RoPE.

visual.title: Position information
visual.caption: Attention alone is permutation-invariant; positional information tells the model where tokens occur in the sequence.

lessons.title: Language Modeling & Next-token Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: A causal language model estimates the probability of each next token conditioned on previous tokens and trains using cross-entropy over sequences. Generation repeatedly samples or selects from the predicted distribution.

lessons.title: Autoencoders & VAEs
lessons.interviewAnswer: A standard autoencoder learns a compressed code for reconstruction. A VAE regularizes the latent distribution and samples from it, enabling generation but introducing a reconstruction–regularization trade-off.

visual.title: Variational autoencoder
visual.caption: A VAE learns a structured latent distribution by combining reconstruction quality with a KL regularization term.

lessons.title: VQ-VAE / VQGAN & Vector Quantization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Vector quantization maps continuous encoder features to entries in a discrete codebook. VQGAN combines discrete compression with perceptual/adversarial objectives to improve reconstructed visual quality.

visual.title: Vector-quantized autoencoder
visual.caption: Vector quantization replaces continuous latents with discrete codebook entries; adversarial/perceptual losses improve visual fidelity.

lessons.title: GAN Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A GAN trains a generator to fool a discriminator while the discriminator learns to distinguish real from generated samples. This adversarial game can produce sharp images but may be unstable.

visual.title: GAN training game
visual.caption: The generator learns to fool the discriminator while the discriminator learns to distinguish generated from real samples.

lessons.title: CycleGAN & Unpaired Translation
lessons.interviewAnswer: CycleGAN learns mappings between two unpaired image domains using adversarial losses plus cycle consistency. The cycle constraint encourages content preservation but does not guarantee physical correctness or eliminate hallucination.

visual.title: CycleGAN
visual.caption: Cycle consistency encourages an unpaired translation A→B→A to preserve information from the original sample.

lessons.title: Diffusion Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: Diffusion models learn to reverse a progressive corruption process. During generation they start from noise and iteratively move toward a sample from the learned data distribution.

visual.title: Diffusion generation
visual.caption: Training learns the reverse of a gradual corruption process; sampling repeatedly removes noise from an initial random state.

lessons.title: Latent Diffusion
lessons.interviewAnswer: Latent diffusion performs the generative process in a compressed latent space rather than pixels, reducing compute while a decoder maps the final latent back to the image domain.

visual.title: Latent diffusion
visual.caption: Moving diffusion from pixel space into a compressed latent space reduces compute while preserving generative capacity.

lessons.title: Flow Matching
lessons.interviewAnswer: Flow matching trains a model to predict a continuous velocity field that transports samples from a simple distribution such as noise toward the data distribution. Inference integrates that learned vector field over time.

visual.title: Flow matching
visual.caption: Flow matching learns a continuous vector field that transports noise toward the data distribution.

lessons.title: Conditioning & Classifier-Free Guidance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Conditioning provides control information such as text, labels, embeddings or structural inputs. Classifier-free guidance combines conditioned and unconditioned predictions to strengthen adherence to the condition.

visual.title: Conditional generation
visual.caption: Conditioning steers generation using text, labels, images, structural signals or learned embeddings.

lessons.title: ControlNet
lessons.interviewAnswer: ControlNet adds a trainable conditioning branch to a pretrained diffusion model so structural signals such as edges, depth or poses can guide generation while preserving much of the pretrained backbone.

visual.title: ControlNet conditioning
visual.caption: ControlNet injects spatial control into a pretrained diffusion backbone while preserving the original generative model.

lessons.title: GAN vs Diffusion vs Flow Matching
lessons.interviewAnswer: GANs use adversarial training and usually sample in one/few passes; diffusion learns a reverse corruption process; flow matching learns a transport velocity field. Compare them by stability, sample quality/diversity, inference speed and controllability—not by a single winner.

visual.title: GAN vs Diffusion vs Flow Matching
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering
lessons.interviewAnswer: Good prompting specifies the task, context, constraints and output format, then evaluates prompts on representative examples. Prompting should be treated as an engineering artifact with tests, not magic wording.

lessons.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
lessons.interviewAnswer: RAG retrieves relevant external context and supplies it to the model at generation time. A reliable RAG system depends on ingestion, chunking, embeddings, retrieval, reranking, context construction and evaluation—not only the LLM.

visual.title: RAG pipeline
visual.caption: RAG separates knowledge retrieval from generation so answers can use external, updateable evidence.

lessons.title: Embedding Search & Vector Databases
lessons.interviewAnswer: Convert documents and queries to embeddings, compare them using a similarity metric, and retrieve nearest items. Production retrieval often adds metadata filters, hybrid lexical search and reranking.

visual.title: Embedding retrieval
visual.caption: Semantic retrieval compares learned vector representations rather than exact term overlap.

lessons.title: RAG Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval metrics ask whether relevant evidence was found; generation metrics assess faithfulness, relevance and task success. Human or domain evaluation remains important.

visual.title: RAG Evaluation
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Tool / Function Calling
lessons.interviewAnswer: Tool calling lets the model choose structured actions while deterministic code performs calculations, database access or external operations. The model orchestrates; the tool remains the source of truth for precise operations.

visual.title: Tool calling
visual.caption: The LLM orchestrates; deterministic systems remain responsible for calculations, database access or side effects.

lessons.title: Agents & LangGraph
lessons.interviewAnswer: An agent repeatedly observes state, chooses an action/tool, updates state and decides whether to continue. Graph-based orchestration makes control flow, retries and state transitions explicit.

visual.title: Agent loop
visual.caption: An agent repeatedly chooses actions based on intermediate observations instead of producing one fixed response.

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
lessons.interviewAnswer: MCP standardizes how AI applications discover and invoke external tools/resources through a common protocol, reducing one-off integrations between assistants and services.

visual.title: MCP architecture
visual.caption: MCP standardizes how AI clients discover and invoke external capabilities through a common protocol.

lessons.title: LLM Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Define task-specific datasets and success criteria, then combine deterministic checks, model-based judges where appropriate, and human review. Track quality, latency, cost and safety together.

visual.title: LLM Evaluation
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: LLM Inference: Temperature, Top-p, KV Cache
lessons.interviewAnswer: Temperature and top-p affect sampling randomness; the KV cache reuses attention keys/values from previous tokens to avoid recomputing the entire prefix during autoregressive generation.

visual.title: LLM inference path
visual.caption: Serving separates prompt prefill from token-by-token decode; KV caching avoids recomputing past attention states.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning, LoRA & Quantization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Fine-tuning changes model behavior through training; LoRA learns low-rank adapter updates instead of all parameters; quantization reduces numerical precision to lower memory/compute, usually with some quality trade-off.

visual.title: LoRA adaptation
visual.caption: LoRA learns a low-rank update while keeping the large pretrained weight matrix frozen.

lessons.title: Graph ML Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A graph represents entities as nodes and relationships as edges. ML on graphs combines node/edge features with graph structure to predict node labels, links, graph properties or rankings.

visual.title: Graph representation
visual.caption: Graphs represent entities as nodes and relationships as edges; node/edge features add attributes.

lessons.title: Message Passing in GNNs
lessons.interviewAnswer: GNN layers aggregate information from neighbors and combine it with the current node representation. Repeating layers expands the receptive field over graph hops.

visual.title: GNN message passing
visual.caption: GNN layers repeatedly aggregate information from local neighborhoods.

lessons.title: GraphSAGE
lessons.interviewAnswer: GraphSAGE learns aggregation functions that combine sampled neighbor features, enabling inductive embeddings for nodes that were not present during training.

visual.title: GraphSAGE
visual.caption: GraphSAGE is inductive because the aggregation function can embed previously unseen nodes from features and neighborhoods.

lessons.title: Link Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Link prediction scores whether an edge should exist between two nodes. Candidate node embeddings are combined with a scoring function and trained against positive and negative edges.

lessons.title: Recall@K & Ranking Evaluation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Recall@K asks whether relevant items appear in the top K recommendations. It fits reviewer/recommender systems better than plain classification accuracy because users receive ranked candidates.

lessons.title: Popularity Bias in Recommenders
lessons.interviewAnswer: Highly active/popular entities can dominate recommendations even when niche specialists are more relevant. Mitigation can include debiasing, re-ranking, diversity constraints or separating expertise from activity.

visual.title: Popularity bias
visual.caption: Interaction data is often dominated by popular items, which can cause recommenders to over-recommend the head unless corrected.

lessons.title: ETL vs ELT
lessons.interviewAnswer: ETL transforms data before loading it into the target system; ELT loads raw data first and transforms within a powerful warehouse/lakehouse. Choice depends on governance, scale, latency and platform.

visual.title: ETL vs ELT
visual.caption: The choice depends on compute location, governance, latency and how many downstream consumers need raw data.

lessons.title: Batch vs Streaming
lessons.interviewAnswer: Batch processing handles bounded datasets on a schedule; streaming processes events continuously or in small increments. Choose based on freshness requirements, complexity, cost and correctness needs.

visual.title: Batch vs streaming
visual.caption: Many systems combine both: streaming for freshness and batch for recomputation/backfills.

lessons.title: Kafka Fundamentals
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kafka is a distributed event log. Producers write records to partitioned topics; consumers read offsets, often in consumer groups for parallelism and fault tolerance.

visual.title: Kafka data flow
visual.caption: Kafka decouples producers and consumers through durable ordered partition logs.

lessons.title: Flink & Stateful Stream Processing
lessons.interviewAnswer: Flink processes unbounded streams with state, event-time semantics, windows and checkpointing. It is designed for continuous computations where correctness across time and failures matters.

visual.title: Stateful stream processing
visual.caption: Flink processes unbounded streams with state, event-time semantics and fault-tolerant checkpoints.

lessons.title: Spark / PySpark
lessons.interviewAnswer: Spark distributes transformations over partitions of large datasets. DataFrames and Spark SQL provide optimized execution while lazy evaluation lets Spark build an execution plan before running actions.

visual.title: Spark execution
visual.caption: Spark builds a lazy computation plan and distributes stages/tasks across executors.

lessons.title: Workflow Orchestration
lessons.interviewAnswer: Orchestrators schedule and coordinate multi-step workflows, track dependencies, retries and failures, and separate workflow control from transformation logic.

visual.title: Workflow orchestration
visual.caption: Orchestrators encode dependencies, retries, schedules and observability across multi-step data/ML workflows.

lessons.title: Data Quality & Schema Evolution
lessons.interviewAnswer: Production pipelines should validate schema, ranges, null rates, uniqueness and business constraints. Schema changes need explicit compatibility and migration strategies rather than silent breakage.

lessons.title: Production ML Pipeline
lessons.interviewAnswer: A production ML pipeline reliably connects data ingestion and validation to preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, deployment, inference and monitoring. The key difference from a notebook is repeatability, observability and failure handling.

visual.title: Production ML lifecycle
visual.caption: Production ML is a continuous system around the model, not only a training script.

lessons.title: Experiment Tracking
lessons.interviewAnswer: Track code version, data version, hyperparameters, environment, metrics and artifacts so experiments can be reproduced and compared. A checkpoint without its context is not a reproducible experiment.

lessons.title: Model Registry & Versioning
lessons.interviewAnswer: A model registry stores versioned model artifacts plus metadata, evaluation results and lifecycle state. It gives deployment systems an explicit, auditable model version to promote or roll back.

visual.title: Model registry lifecycle
visual.caption: A registry links each model version to metadata, evaluation and deployment status so releases are reproducible and reversible.

lessons.title: Batch vs Online Model Serving
lessons.interviewAnswer: Online serving optimizes low-latency per-request predictions; batch inference processes many items asynchronously and is often simpler and cheaper for heavy workloads. Choose from user and freshness requirements.

visual.title: Batch vs online inference
visual.caption: Serving architecture should follow latency, freshness, throughput and cost requirements.

lessons.title: APIs around ML Models
lessons.interviewAnswer: An API validates requests, invokes preprocessing and inference, then returns predictions or a job ID. Keep model logic separate from transport/UI so each layer can scale and evolve independently.

lessons.title: Monitoring: System, Data & Model
lessons.interviewAnswer: Monitor system health such as failures and latency, data quality/drift, and model quality when ground truth becomes available. Version models so a degraded release can be rolled back.

visual.title: ML monitoring stack
visual.caption: Monitoring needs multiple layers because infrastructure can be healthy while the model or product outcome degrades.

lessons.title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data drift means the input distribution changes; concept drift means the relationship between inputs and target changes. Drift detection is a signal to investigate—not automatic proof that retraining is needed.

visual.title: Distribution drift
visual.caption: Drift means production inputs/predictions differ from the reference distribution; it does not automatically imply worse model quality.

lessons.title: Canary, Blue/Green & Shadow Deployment
lessons.interviewAnswer: Canary sends a small share of live traffic to the new model, blue/green switches between parallel environments, and shadow deployment mirrors traffic to a new model without using its outputs for users.

visual.title: Deployment strategies
visual.caption: Safe model releases separate deployment from full traffic exposure.

lessons.title: CI/CD for ML
lessons.interviewAnswer: CI validates code, data contracts and model tests on change; CD automates safe packaging and deployment after gates. ML adds artifact/data/model validation beyond normal software tests.

visual.title: CI/CD for ML
visual.caption: ML delivery pipelines must validate both software correctness and data/model behavior.

lessons.title: Docker Images & Containers
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Docker image is an immutable package containing application code, runtime and dependencies; a container is a running instance of that image. Containers make the inference environment portable and reproducible.

visual.title: Docker image to container
visual.caption: An image packages filesystem + metadata; a container is a running instance of that image.

lessons.title: Dockerizing an ML Inference Service
lessons.interviewAnswer: Package preprocessing, inference code and dependencies in an image. The model checkpoint can be baked into the image for simplicity or loaded from object storage/volume when versioning and image size matter.

visual.title: Dockerizing an ML Inference Service
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Docker Compose
lessons.interviewAnswer: Compose defines a multi-container application—such as API, database, Kafka, Redis and workers—in one declarative file. Multiple containers may reuse the same image with different commands.

visual.title: Docker Compose services
visual.caption: Compose defines multiple containers, networks, volumes and startup dependencies as one local application stack.

lessons.title: Kubernetes for ML Services
lessons.interviewAnswer: Kubernetes schedules containers across a cluster and provides deployments, services, scaling and rolling updates. Use it when operational complexity and scale justify the platform overhead.

visual.title: Kubernetes abstraction
visual.caption: Kubernetes keeps desired replicas running and exposes them through stable service networking.

lessons.title: Cloud Primitives for Production ML
lessons.interviewAnswer: Cloud ML systems are easier to reason about by capability: object storage for data/artifacts, a container registry, scalable compute, managed training/serving, orchestration, observability, identity/networking and a model/metadata layer. AWS, Azure and GCP expose different products for these same architectural needs.

visual.title: AWS ML platform map
visual.caption: Cloud services are building blocks; choose the minimum set that matches the workload rather than memorizing product names.

lessons.title: Cross-Cloud Mapping: AWS, Azure & GCP
lessons.interviewAnswer: Map cloud services by responsibility rather than forcing exact equivalents. S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage all provide object storage; ECR, ACR and Artifact Registry store images/artifacts; SageMaker, Azure Machine Learning and Vertex AI cover overlapping managed ML lifecycle capabilities, while container, workflow and observability services differ in boundaries and semantics.

visual.title: Azure ↔ AWS concept mapping
visual.caption: Concepts transfer across clouds, while service APIs, IAM, networking and operational details differ.

lessons.title: IAM, Secrets & Least Privilege
lessons.interviewAnswer: Production services should receive only the permissions they need, with credentials kept in secret-management mechanisms rather than source code or images. Identity and network boundaries are part of ML system design.

lessons.title: ML System Design Interview Framework
lessons.interviewAnswer: Start with product requirements and constraints, then define data, labels, metrics, baseline, training pipeline, serving path, storage, scale, monitoring, failure modes and iteration loop. Architecture should follow requirements—not precede them.

visual.title: ML system design sequence
visual.caption: Architecture should follow product requirements, constraints and failure costs—not precede them.

lessons.title: Design a Recommendation System
lessons.interviewAnswer: Clarify candidate generation, ranking objective, feedback signals, cold start, popularity bias and top-k evaluation. Often use a two-stage architecture: fast candidate retrieval followed by richer ranking.

visual.title: Recommender system
visual.caption: A production recommender separates candidate generation from richer ranking and closes the loop with interaction feedback.

lessons.title: Design an Internal RAG Assistant
lessons.interviewAnswer: Define document sources and permissions, ingestion/chunking, embeddings and indexes, retrieval/reranking, prompt construction, citations, evaluation, latency/cost and monitoring. Security boundaries matter as much as answer quality.

visual.title: Production RAG
visual.caption: A production RAG system needs ingestion, retrieval quality, security and evaluation—not just an LLM call.

lessons.title: Design an Image Reconstruction Service
lessons.interviewAnswer: For heavy image/3D inference, prefer asynchronous job submission: upload input, validate, enqueue work, run GPU inference, store outputs, expose job status, and monitor latency/failures/quality.

visual.title: Image inference service
visual.caption: Heavy image workloads often use asynchronous jobs instead of holding a synchronous request open.

lessons.title: Design a Rare-event Detection System
lessons.interviewAnswer: Clarify the cost of false negatives/positives, label delay, class imbalance and response-time requirement. Optimize the operating threshold around business risk and monitor drift plus delayed ground truth.

visual.title: Fraud detection system
visual.caption: Fraud systems combine low latency with asymmetric error costs, human review and delayed ground truth.

lessons.title: Latency, Throughput & Cost Trade-offs
lessons.interviewAnswer: Latency is time per request; throughput is work per unit time. Batching usually improves throughput/GPU utilization but can increase individual-request latency, so tune around the product SLO and cost.

visual.title: Latency, Throughput & Cost Trade-offs
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Failure Modes & Graceful Degradation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Design what happens when the model, dependency or input fails: validate early, use timeouts/retries carefully, support fallback behavior, isolate failures and keep enough observability to diagnose them.

lessons.title: Case Study: Scientific 3D Reconstruction / Super-resolution
lessons.interviewAnswer: Lead with the physical problem and downstream use, then explain the 2D/3D constraint, model stages, interpolation/fusion, your contribution and validation. Be explicit about hallucination risk and what the domain expert validated.

visual.title: Scientific 3D reconstruction case
visual.caption: A robust reconstruction system separates enhancement from fusion and validates the result with both image and domain-specific checks.

lessons.title: Case Study: Graph-based Matching & Recommendation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Explain why the problem is naturally a graph, how semantic PR features enter the graph, why an inductive GNN helps new PRs, how link prediction/ranking is evaluated and how popularity bias is handled.

visual.title: Reviewer recommendation graph
visual.caption: Historical developer–PR relations plus semantic PR features create a graph space for reviewer recommendation.

lessons.title: Case Study: Real-time Streaming Application
lessons.interviewAnswer: Describe event source → Kafka → stream processor → storage/cache/API → UI. Explain why streaming was needed, what each component owns, how containers communicate and where failures are observed.

visual.title: Streaming monitoring case
visual.caption: The case demonstrates event streaming, stateful processing, caching and an end-user visualization layer.

lessons.title: Case Study: LLM Copilot with Tools + RAG
lessons.interviewAnswer: Keep numerical/business logic deterministic in tools, use the LLM for orchestration and explanation, use RAG only for unstructured knowledge, and evaluate tool correctness separately from language quality.

visual.title: LLM copilot case
visual.caption: The LLM orchestrates and explains while deterministic tools remain the numerical source of truth.

lessons.title: Time-Series Splits & Backtesting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Random train/test splitting is usually wrong for forecasting because it leaks the future into the past. I split chronologically and evaluate with rolling or expanding-window backtests that mimic how the model will actually be used.

visual.title: Rolling-origin validation
visual.caption: Time-series validation respects chronology; random shuffling can leak future information.

lessons.title: Stationarity, ACF & PACF
lessons.interviewAnswer: Stationarity means the statistical behavior of a series is stable enough over time for many classical models to learn consistent relationships. I inspect trend/seasonality and autocorrelation; differencing or transformation can help when the level is non-stationary.

visual.title: Autocorrelation by lag
visual.caption: The ACF summarizes correlation between a series and lagged versions of itself; slow decay can signal persistent structure.

lessons.title: ARIMA / SARIMA
lessons.interviewAnswer: ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing and moving-average error terms. The p,d,q orders control lagged values, differencing and lagged forecast errors; SARIMA adds seasonal equivalents. I use it as a strong interpretable baseline when temporal dependence is meaningful.

visual.title: ARIMA reasoning
visual.caption: ARIMA combines autoregression, differencing and moving-average error structure.

lessons.title: Exponential Smoothing / ETS
lessons.interviewAnswer: Exponential smoothing builds forecasts from recursively updated level, trend and seasonality components, giving more weight to recent observations. ETS models are excellent business-forecasting baselines, especially when patterns are smooth and recurring.

visual.title: Exponential smoothing intuition
visual.caption: Recent observations receive more weight; the smoothing parameter controls responsiveness.

lessons.title: Forecasting Metrics & Baselines
lessons.interviewAnswer: For forecasts I choose metrics based on business cost and scale. MAE is easy to interpret, RMSE emphasizes large misses, MAPE can break near zero, and scaled metrics like MASE help compare across series. I always compare against naive and seasonal-naive baselines.

visual.title: Forecasting Metrics & Baselines
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Prophet & Decomposable Forecasting
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prophet models a series as trend plus seasonality plus holiday/event effects. I use it when those components match the problem and fast, interpretable forecasting matters, but I still compare it with simpler and stronger baselines rather than treating it as universally best.

lessons.title: Causal Inference vs Prediction
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prediction asks what will happen; causal inference asks what would happen if we intervene. A predictive feature can be highly correlated with an outcome without being a valid lever. Causal answers require assumptions about treatment assignment, confounding and counterfactuals.

lessons.title: DAGs, Confounders & Colliders
lessons.interviewAnswer: A causal DAG encodes assumptions about which variables cause which others. A confounder causes both treatment and outcome and often needs adjustment; a collider is caused by two variables and conditioning on it can create a spurious association.

visual.title: Confounder vs collider
visual.caption: A confounder creates a backdoor path that often needs adjustment. Conditioning on a collider can create bias.

lessons.title: Profiling & Benchmarking ML Systems
lessons.interviewAnswer: I optimize only after measuring. I separate data loading, preprocessing, host-to-device transfer, model execution and postprocessing; warm up GPU kernels, synchronize correctly, and report latency distributions plus throughput rather than one timing number.

visual.title: Performance workflow
visual.caption: Optimization begins with measurement; otherwise teams often speed up the wrong component.

lessons.title: Mixed Precision: FP32, FP16 & BF16
lessons.interviewAnswer: Mixed precision runs many expensive operations in FP16 or BF16 while keeping numerically sensitive parts at higher precision. It reduces memory bandwidth and often increases GPU throughput; BF16 has a wider exponent range, while FP16 may need loss scaling during training.

visual.title: Precision trade-off

right.title: FP16/BF16 mixed precision
items: Keep sensitive ops in higher precision

visual.caption: Mixed precision improves throughput when hardware supports it, but numerical stability still needs monitoring.

lessons.title: Quantization for Inference
lessons.interviewAnswer: Quantization represents weights and sometimes activations with fewer bits—such as INT8 or 4-bit—to reduce memory, bandwidth and often latency. Post-training quantization is simpler; quantization-aware training can preserve quality when aggressive quantization hurts accuracy.

visual.title: Post-training quantization
visual.caption: Quantization reduces memory/bandwidth and can accelerate inference at the cost of possible accuracy degradation.

lessons.title: Pruning & Knowledge Distillation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Pruning removes low-value parameters or structure; distillation trains a smaller student to mimic a larger teacher. Both can reduce serving cost, but structured pruning usually maps to hardware better than arbitrary sparsity, and distillation quality depends on the teacher targets and task.

lessons.title: Batching, Queueing & Throughput
lessons.interviewAnswer: Batching amortizes fixed overhead and improves accelerator utilization, so throughput rises, but waiting to form batches can increase latency. I choose static, dynamic or continuous batching based on SLA, traffic pattern and model shape.

visual.title: Batch size trade-off
visual.caption: Larger batches often improve throughput while increasing queueing and per-request latency; dynamic batching balances the two.

lessons.title: Distributed Training: Data & Model Parallelism
lessons.interviewAnswer: Data parallelism replicates the model and splits batches across workers, synchronizing gradients. Model/tensor/pipeline parallelism splits the model when it no longer fits on one device. The right strategy depends on memory, communication cost and model size.

lessons.title: Model Compilation: torch.compile, ONNX & TensorRT
lessons.interviewAnswer: Model compilation captures/lowers computation into optimized kernels or runtimes. torch.compile optimizes PyTorch graphs; ONNX enables portable graph runtimes; TensorRT targets NVIDIA inference. I use them only after profiling and verifying numerical/shape compatibility.

lessons.title: GPU Memory: Parameters, Activations & KV Cache
lessons.interviewAnswer: GPU memory is consumed by parameters, activations, gradients, optimizer states and temporary workspaces; LLM inference also spends heavily on KV cache. I estimate which term dominates before deciding between smaller batches, checkpointing, quantization or sharding.

visual.title: GPU memory budget
visual.caption: Training memory includes far more than model weights; serving memory is often dominated by weights and KV cache.

lessons.title: Responsible AI: Risk, Impact & Governance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Responsible AI means identifying who can be harmed, how failures are measured, what human oversight exists, and how risks are monitored throughout the lifecycle. I treat it as an engineering requirement, not a final compliance checklist.

lessons.title: Bias & Fairness in ML
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bias can enter through sampling, labels, features, historical decisions or deployment feedback. Fairness has multiple incompatible definitions, so I first identify the affected groups and harm, then choose metrics/interventions aligned with the use case.

lessons.title: Privacy, PII & Data Minimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: I minimize sensitive data, define purpose and retention, restrict access, encrypt data in transit/at rest, and avoid sending PII to models or logs unless explicitly required and governed. Privacy starts in architecture, not with masking at the end.

visual.title: Privacy, PII & Data Minimization
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Prompt Injection & Tool Abuse
lessons.interviewAnswer: Prompt injection is when untrusted content manipulates the model into ignoring intended instructions or misusing tools. I assume model instructions are not a security boundary: constrain tools with permissions, validate arguments, separate trusted/untrusted data and require confirmation for sensitive actions.

visual.title: Prompt-injection attack path
items: Malicious instruction competes with system goal
visual.caption: Treat retrieved/user content as data, not authority; tools need explicit permission boundaries and validation.

lessons.title: RAG Security & Access Control
lessons.interviewAnswer: RAG security requires authorization-aware ingestion and retrieval, not only good prompts. I preserve document permissions as metadata, filter before retrieval, isolate tenants, sanitize untrusted content and test for indirect prompt injection and data exfiltration.

visual.title: RAG security layers
visual.caption: RAG security spans ingestion, retrieval permissions, model context and downstream actions.

lessons.title: Model & Dependency Supply-Chain Security
lessons.interviewAnswer: Model artifacts, packages, containers and datasets are executable/trusted inputs to an AI system. I pin and scan dependencies, verify model provenance/checksums, avoid unsafe deserialization, use trusted registries and keep an SBOM where appropriate.

lessons.title: AI Red Teaming & Adversarial Testing
lessons.interviewAnswer: Red teaming deliberately searches for failure modes outside normal test cases: prompt injection, harmful outputs, data leakage, jailbreaks, tool misuse and robustness failures. I convert discovered attacks into repeatable regression tests.

lessons.title: Guardrails, Policy Checks & AI Observability
lessons.interviewAnswer: Guardrails are deterministic or model-assisted checks around an AI system: input validation, output schemas, policy classifiers, tool permissions, rate limits and human approval. Observability records traces, retrieval/tool calls, latency, cost and safety events so failures can be diagnosed.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-Loop & Safe Fallbacks
lessons.interviewAnswer: Human-in-the-loop is useful when errors are costly, uncertainty can be detected and a qualified reviewer can actually improve decisions. I define escalation thresholds, what context the human sees, and a safe fallback when the model or reviewer is unavailable.

visual.title: Human-in-the-loop decision
visual.caption: Human review is most useful when routing rules are explicit and feedback returns to the system.

lessons.title: RL Fundamentals: Agent, Environment, State, Action & Reward
lessons.interviewAnswer: Reinforcement learning is sequential decision-making by interaction. An agent observes a state, chooses an action using a policy, receives a reward and transitions to a new state. The objective is not immediate reward alone, but maximizing expected cumulative return over time.

visual.title: Agent–environment loop
visual.caption: Reinforcement learning optimizes long-term return through repeated interaction with an environment.

lessons.title: Value Functions & the Bellman Equation
lessons.interviewAnswer: A value function estimates expected future return. V(s) values a state under a policy; Q(s,a) values taking an action in a state and then following the policy. The Bellman equation expresses a value recursively as immediate reward plus discounted expected value of the next state.

visual.title: Bellman backup
visual.caption: The Bellman equation expresses value recursively as immediate reward plus discounted future value.

lessons.title: Exploration vs Exploitation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Exploitation chooses actions that currently look best; exploration tries uncertain actions to learn whether something better exists. RL needs a balance because pure exploitation can lock into a suboptimal policy, while excessive exploration wastes reward or can be unsafe.

visual.title: Exploration vs exploitation
visual.caption: Good RL policies balance learning about the environment with using what is already known.

lessons.title: Q-learning & Deep Q-Networks
lessons.interviewAnswer: Q-learning learns the action-value function using the target r + γ max Q(s′,a′), so it can learn the greedy optimal policy from off-policy experience. DQN replaces a tabular Q-function with a neural network and stabilizes training using experience replay and a target network.

visual.title: Q-learning update
visual.caption: Q-learning is off-policy because the target uses the best next action regardless of the behavior action.

lessons.title: Policy Gradients
lessons.interviewAnswer: Policy-gradient methods optimize policy parameters directly. REINFORCE increases the log-probability of actions that produced high return and decreases it for poor return. This handles stochastic and continuous policies naturally, but raw Monte Carlo gradients can have high variance.

lessons.title: Actor-Critic & Advantage Estimation
lessons.interviewAnswer: Actor-critic combines a policy model—the actor—with a value model—the critic. The critic estimates how good the current state/action is, and the actor updates using an advantage signal, which reduces the high variance of pure Monte Carlo policy gradients.

visual.title: Actor–critic
visual.caption: Actor–critic methods combine direct policy optimization with learned value estimates.

lessons.title: PPO & Stable Policy Optimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: PPO is an on-policy actor-critic algorithm that limits how aggressively the policy changes. It uses a probability-ratio objective with clipping, so updates that move too far from the data-collecting policy stop receiving extra benefit. That usually makes policy optimization more stable and practical.

visual.title: PPO update
visual.caption: PPO limits destructive policy updates with a clipped objective while remaining relatively simple to implement.

lessons.title: RLHF, Reward Models & Preference Optimization
lessons.interviewAnswer: RLHF usually starts with supervised instruction tuning, then learns a preference or reward signal from human comparisons and optimizes the policy against that signal while constraining drift from a reference model. PPO is one optimization route; DPO is different—it directly optimizes preference likelihood without explicitly training a reward model and running online RL.

visual.title: Preference optimization pipeline
visual.caption: Preference optimization aligns model behavior with ranked outputs rather than only next-token likelihood.

lessons.title: Multimodal AI Fundamentals & Fusion
lessons.interviewAnswer: Multimodal models combine information from different modalities such as text, images, audio or video. The core problems are representation, alignment and fusion: encode each modality, place or project representations into a compatible space, and let the model combine them for prediction or generation.

lessons.title: CLIP & Contrastive Image–Text Alignment
lessons.interviewAnswer: CLIP trains an image encoder and text encoder so matched image-caption pairs have high cosine similarity and mismatched pairs have lower similarity. A contrastive loss over a batch creates a shared embedding space, which enables zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval.

visual.title: CLIP contrastive learning
visual.caption: CLIP pulls matched image/text embeddings together and pushes mismatched pairs apart with a contrastive objective.

lessons.title: Vision-Language Model Architecture: Encoder, Projector & LLM
lessons.interviewAnswer: A common VLM architecture uses a pretrained vision encoder to turn an image into visual features, a projector or resampler to map those features into the language model’s embedding space, and an LLM that attends to the resulting visual tokens together with text tokens to generate an answer.

visual.title: Vision-language model
visual.caption: A VLM converts visual information into token-like representations that a language model can condition on.

lessons.title: Visual Instruction Tuning & LLaVA
lessons.interviewAnswer: Visual instruction tuning adapts a vision-language model to follow natural-language instructions grounded in images. LLaVA is a classic example: it connects a CLIP vision encoder to an LLM through a projector and trains on image-instruction-response data so the model learns conversational visual reasoning.

lessons.title: Multimodal Tokenization, Patches & Resamplers
lessons.interviewAnswer: Text becomes discrete tokens, while images are usually represented as patches or learned visual features. A multimodal model must convert those features into a manageable token sequence—often through patch embeddings, pooling, learned queries, a Q-Former or a Perceiver-style resampler—before the language model consumes them.

lessons.title: Multimodal Evaluation & Visual Hallucination
lessons.interviewAnswer: Multimodal evaluation should test whether the answer is actually grounded in the image, not only whether the text is fluent. I evaluate task accuracy plus grounding/OCR/counting/spatial reasoning slices, hallucination rates and robustness to irrelevant or missing visual information.

lessons.title: Speech & Audio Transformers: Spectrograms and ASR
lessons.interviewAnswer: Audio models typically convert a waveform into time-frequency features such as log-Mel spectrograms, then use an encoder or encoder-decoder model to classify audio or generate text. Whisper is a well-known transformer encoder-decoder trained for multilingual speech recognition, translation and language identification.

lessons.title: Big-O Time & Space Complexity
lessons.interviewAnswer: Big-O describes how runtime or memory grows with input size. I use it to compare algorithms asymptotically, while remembering constants, cache behavior and real input sizes still matter in practice.
keyPoints: Know O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²).
Distinguish worst, average and amortized complexity.

visual.title: Growth rates as input size increases
visual.caption: Conceptual growth: asymptotic complexity matters as data size scales.

lessons.title: Hash Tables, Sets & Dictionaries
lessons.interviewAnswer: Hash tables provide average O(1) insert and lookup by mapping keys to buckets; collisions are resolved internally. They are fundamental for joins, deduplication, counting and caches.
keyPoints: Sets are useful for membership and uniqueness.

lessons.title: Stacks, Queues & Heaps
lessons.interviewAnswer: Stacks are LIFO, queues FIFO, and heaps maintain fast access to an extreme element. They solve different ordering problems and show up in graph traversal, streaming and top-k systems.
keyPoints: Heap: O(log n) insert/pop, O(1) peek.

lessons.title: Trees, Graph Traversal, BFS & DFS
lessons.interviewAnswer: BFS explores level by level and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS explores depth-first and is useful for connectivity, cycles and recursive structure.
keyPoints: Represent graphs with adjacency lists for sparse data.
BFS uses a queue; DFS uses stack/recursion.

lessons.title: Sorting, Binary Search & Selection
lessons.interviewAnswer: Sorting enables ordered scans and binary search; binary search reduces lookup in sorted data to O(log n). Selection/top-k can often avoid sorting the entire dataset.
keyPoints: Binary search requires an ordered monotonic condition.
Comparison sorting has O(n log n) general lower bound.
Top-k may use heaps or partition algorithms.

lessons.title: Sampling & Streaming Algorithms
lessons.interviewAnswer: When data is too large to hold in memory, streaming algorithms maintain compact summaries such as reservoir samples, sketches or approximate counts.
keyPoints: Reservoir sampling gives an unbiased fixed-size sample from a stream.
Approximate sketches trade small error for bounded memory.

lessons.title: A Systematic EDA Workflow
lessons.interviewAnswer: EDA should answer what the rows/columns mean, whether values are valid, how variables are distributed, how missingness occurs, and which relationships or subgroups deserve deeper investigation before modeling.
keyPoints: Start with schema, units and provenance.
Check duplicates, impossible values and leakage.

visual.title: EDA loop
visual.caption: EDA is an iterative diagnostic process, not a collection of decorative plots.

lessons.title: Distributions, Skewness & Outliers
lessons.interviewAnswer: Outliers are not automatically bad data. I first determine whether they are errors, rare but valid cases, or a separate population, then choose transformations, robust statistics or explicit modeling accordingly.
keyPoints: Compare mean vs median under skew.
Log transforms can stabilize heavy right tails.

visual.title: Outlier detection depends on context
visual.caption: An unusual point may be an error, a rare valid case, or the most important observation in the dataset.

lessons.title: Missingness: MCAR, MAR & MNAR
lessons.interviewAnswer: Missing values can be completely random, explainable by observed variables, or related to the missing value itself. The mechanism matters because naive imputation can bias estimates and hide useful missingness signals.
keyPoints: MAR: missingness depends on observed variables.
MNAR: missingness depends on unobserved/missing value.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Statistical Visualization
lessons.interviewAnswer: Choose charts based on the question: distributions, comparisons, relationships, composition or change over time. Favor position and length over harder-to-compare encodings and avoid decorative choices that distort magnitude.

visual.title: Match mark to question
visual.caption: Position and length are usually easier to compare accurately than angle or area; choose encodings to match the analytical task.

lessons.title: Misleading Charts & Visualization Pitfalls
lessons.interviewAnswer: A visualization can be numerically correct and still mislead through truncated axes, inappropriate aggregation, dual axes, area encodings or selective time windows.
keyPoints: Preserve meaningful baselines when magnitude comparisons matter.

lessons.title: GroupBy, Pivot & Cohort Analysis
lessons.interviewAnswer: Grouping and pivoting turn event-level data into interpretable segment, cohort and time summaries. The key is choosing denominators and cohorts consistently.
keyPoints: Do not mix counts and rates without denominators.

lessons.title: Sampling Distributions & Standard Error
lessons.interviewAnswer: A sampling distribution describes how an estimator would vary across repeated samples. Standard error measures that estimator uncertainty; it is not the standard deviation of the raw observations.
keyPoints: Estimator variability shrinks with more information/sample size.
SE and population SD answer different questions.

visual.title: Sampling Distributions & Standard Error
items: Estimator variability shrinks with more information/sample size.
SE and population SD answer different questions.
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Bootstrap & Resampling
lessons.interviewAnswer: The bootstrap approximates an estimator’s sampling distribution by repeatedly resampling the observed dataset with replacement. It is useful when analytic standard errors are difficult but the sample is reasonably representative.
keyPoints: Use the empirical distribution for uncertainty.

visual.title: Bootstrap workflow
visual.caption: Bootstrap approximates sampling uncertainty using repeated resamples of the observed data.

lessons.title: Permutation & Randomization Tests
lessons.interviewAnswer: A permutation test builds a null distribution by shuffling labels in a way justified by exchangeability under the null. It is especially useful for transparent nonparametric testing.
keyPoints: Shuffle only under a valid exchangeability assumption.
p-value is the tail probability under the randomization/null procedure.

lessons.title: Multiple Testing & False Discovery Rate
lessons.interviewAnswer: When many hypotheses are tested, false positives accumulate. Family-wise methods such as Bonferroni control any false positive; FDR methods such as Benjamini–Hochberg control the expected proportion among discoveries.
keyPoints: More tests → more opportunities for false positives.
FWER and FDR are different guarantees.

visual.title: Why multiple testing matters
visual.caption: With many independent tests, the chance of at least one false positive rises quickly if per-test α is unchanged.

lessons.title: Effect Size vs Statistical Significance
lessons.interviewAnswer: Statistical significance asks whether an effect is hard to explain by noise under a null; effect size asks whether the magnitude is practically meaningful. Large samples can make tiny effects significant.
keyPoints: Report magnitude and uncertainty, not p-value alone.
Practical significance depends on costs/base rates.
Confidence intervals communicate plausible effect ranges.

visual.title: Effect Size vs Statistical Significance
items: Report magnitude and uncertainty, not p-value alone.
Practical significance depends on costs/base rates.
Confidence intervals communicate plausible effect ranges.
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: ANOVA & Comparing Multiple Groups
lessons.interviewAnswer: ANOVA tests whether group means differ more than expected from within-group variability under model assumptions. A significant omnibus test does not say which groups differ, so post-hoc comparisons require care.
keyPoints: Assumptions include independence and model-specific variance/error structure.

lessons.title: Chi-square Tests for Categorical Data
lessons.interviewAnswer: Chi-square tests compare observed categorical counts with counts expected under a null such as independence. They operate on counts, not percentages detached from sample size.
keyPoints: Expected cell counts matter for approximation quality.

lessons.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
lessons.interviewAnswer: Power is the probability of detecting an effect of a specified size when it truly exists. Sample-size planning links baseline variance/rate, significance level, desired power and minimum detectable effect.
keyPoints: Power is defined relative to an alternative effect size.
Low power produces noisy, inconclusive experiments.

visual.title: Power, Minimum Detectable Effect & Sample Size
items: Power is defined relative to an alternative effect size.
Low power produces noisy, inconclusive experiments.
visual.caption: A compact concept map for the most important ideas in this lesson.

lessons.title: Bayesian Updating: Prior, Likelihood & Posterior
lessons.interviewAnswer: Bayesian inference updates prior beliefs with evidence through the likelihood to produce a posterior distribution. The posterior represents uncertainty about parameters after observing data.
keyPoints: Posterior predictive checks validate consequences of the model.

visual.title: Bayesian update
visual.caption: Bayesian inference updates prior uncertainty with evidence from observed data.

lessons.title: Conjugate Priors
lessons.interviewAnswer: A conjugate prior is chosen so the posterior remains in the same distribution family, giving closed-form updates. It is useful pedagogically and computationally for simple models, though modern Bayesian modeling often uses numerical inference.
keyPoints: Beta-Binomial and Normal-Normal are classic pairs.
Convenience should not override sensible prior modeling.

lessons.title: Credible Intervals vs Confidence Intervals
lessons.interviewAnswer: A Bayesian credible interval is a probability statement about a parameter under the posterior; a frequentist confidence interval is a procedure that covers the fixed parameter at a stated long-run frequency.
keyPoints: Interpretations differ even when numerical intervals look similar.
Frequentist coverage is about repeated procedures.

visual.title: Credible vs confidence intervals
visual.caption: The numerical intervals can look similar while the interpretation is fundamentally different.

lessons.title: MCMC & Posterior Sampling
